newsitem.title: CHINA: New Hong Kong leaders take long view on economy.
newsitem.headline: New Hong Kong leaders take long view on economy.

text.p: Hong Kong's laissez-faire economy has performed just fine in the first month after its historic handover to China, but the territory's new leader Tung Chee-hwa is casting an eye to the future and taking action now.

"I notice there is a major change in that Tung seems to be more concerned with longer-term economic policy than the last phase of the British administration," said Kevin Chan, assistant director at ING Barings.
This is "for the very simple reason that the new government can have more flexibility in setting the land policy in Hong Kong," Chan said.

Hong Kong reverted to Chinese sovereignty on July 1 after 156 years of rule by a foreign power, casting off the title of "British Crown Colony" for "Special Administrative Region" of China, now commonly referred to by its acronym, the SAR.

In the weeks before and after the handover, Tung Chee-hwa, the former shipping magnate chosen by Beijing to guide Hong Kong's future, has repeatedly stressed that Hong Kong people are more interested in "livelihood issues" than in politics.
The most pressing livelihood issue in this crowded territory of 6.4 million people is the provision of housing for the masses as well as the millionaires.
Hong Kong boasts one of the highest per capita incomes in the world but many people cannot afford to buy a home because soaring property values have priced them out of the market.
Tung took aim at this problem in his inaugural speech on July 1, promising to increase the number of residential units significantly over a 10-year period.
Government promises to raise land supply quickly followed.
The prescriptions for a long-term solution to housing supply chilled an overheating real estate market in which prices had risen 30 percent in the first half of the year.

"The SAR is showing its wisdom in calming down Hong Kong's property market. It has so far been mostly a psychological game, but it has worked very well," said Dong Tau, senior regional economist at Schroders Asia Ltd.
The chief executive is expected to elaborate further on his property ideas when he delivers a policy address in October.
Tung has also taken the long view on other issues.
He has vowed to improve the territory's education standards and indicated he will consider the controversial issue of developing an industrial policy to rebuild Hong Kong's manufacturing sector.

Jan Lee, chief economist at Hongkong Bank, said that businesses are also looking further into the future now that the handover has come and gone, taking with it the uncertainty that always accompanies major change and always unsettles markets.

"In the past, there hadn't been that much enthusiasm for investment, despite the noise level. But now people are seeing that the promises of stability will unfold into reality and planning horizons are lengthening," he said.
Economists expect the territory to post healthy growth of around 5.5 percent this year, with inflation of about 6.5 percent. The story should be similar in 1998, they said.
That compares with a growth rate of 4.7 percent and inflation of 6.0 percent for all of 1996.

Latest figures show the economy advanced at a 5.5 percent clip in the fourth quarter of last year, and economists are betting that first-quarter 1997 gross domestic product rose six percent. Prices increased 6.2 percent in the first quarter.
The Hong Kong dollar is seen holding around its HK$7.8 peg to the U.S. dollar despite some recent volatility in the local dollar in the wake of currency instability in the region.
Like other countries in Asia, Hong Kong has seen its currency come under attack recently. But unlike its neighbours, Hong Kong has been able to successfully fend off the assualts.
The economy's underlying strength and the robustness of Hong Kong's financial institutions are credited with keeping the currency afloat.
Moves to rein in the property market are also expected to contribute to the long-term health of the economy, sparing it the sickness that has felled other Asian nations.

"Hopefully over time, this will resolve the worries of the property bubble and the high property exposure of the banks, which is what had happened in Thailand and to a lesser extent in the Philippines and is not a very good thing at all," said Chan.
